title: The Missing Exam Paper
story: Before an exam you print one paper per student, numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on. Afterwards the stack is one paper short: somebody walked out with theirs.
The papers came back in drop-off order. Find the missing number without sorting the pile.
task: Write missingPaper(papers). You printed papers.length + 1 papers, numbered 1 to papers.length + 1. The list holds every number except one, each at most once, in any order. Return the missing number.
If the list is empty, you printed only paper 1, and it is missing.
constraints: All numbers in papers are different, and exactly one number from the range is absent.

examples.explanation: Four papers came back, so five were printed: 1 to 5. Every number except 3 is on the desk.
Four papers were printed. The pile 1, 2, 3 has no gap inside, so the missing one is the last, 4. Looking only for a gap between neighbours would miss this.
Nothing came back, so only paper 1 was printed, and it is missing.

hints: Take [4, 2, 5, 1]. With no paper missing, what would 1 to 5 add up to? What do the four papers add up to?
The full set adds to 15 and the pile to 12. Which paper does the difference stand for? Does the order change either total?
No sorting or storing needed. The total of 1 to m is m × (m + 1) / 2, and one running sum gives the rest.
Let m = papers.length + 1. Start from m × (m + 1) / 2 and subtract each paper in one pass. What is left is the missing number.
bruteForce: For each number from 1 to n + 1, scan the pile for it. The first one you cannot find is the answer.
That is up to n + 1 scans of n papers: about 10 billion reads for 100,000 papers. Sorting and looking for the gap is O(n log n), still more work than needed.

walkthrough: The full set is every number from 1 to m, so you know its total before looking at a paper. Each paper you hold accounts for part of it; the part nobody accounts for is the missing paper.

A hash set also works in O(n) time but costs O(n) memory for a question one number answers. With 100,000 papers the total is about 5 billion: fine for JavaScript numbers and Python integers, but with 32-bit integers you would need a 64-bit type.
solution.timeWhy: One pass over the pile, with one subtraction per paper.
solution.spaceWhy: Only the running total is kept, however many papers there are.
solution.takeaway: When you know exactly what a complete collection contains, compare a summary of it (here, the sum) with the same summary of what you have. The difference points at what is missing.
